body: The Azure portal is a web-based, unified console that gives you a graphical alternative to command-line tools. You can build, manage and monitor everything from simple web apps to complex cloud deployments, and you can create custom dashboards. It runs in a web browser. It is an alternative to command-line tools such as Azure CLI and Azure PowerShell, and it needs no downtime for maintenance.
author: claude

body: Azure Cloud Shell is a browser-based shell for managing Azure resources, and you can open it from the portal. It supports both Azure PowerShell and the Azure CLI, which uses Bash. Azure PowerShell runs cmdlets that call the Azure REST API, while the Azure CLI uses Bash commands. They have similar capabilities and can both be installed on Windows, Linux and Mac, so the choice depends on which language you prefer. Saving commands in a script makes the work repeatable and automatable.
author: claude

body: Azure Arc works with Azure Resource Manager to extend Azure governance, compliance and monitoring to hybrid and multicloud setups. It projects non-Azure resources into Azure Resource Manager so you can manage them like Azure resources, from one consistent platform. Resources it can manage outside Azure include servers, Kubernetes clusters, Azure data services and SQL Server. The goal is familiar Azure management capabilities, regardless of where the resources live.
author: claude

body: Infrastructure as code (IaC) means managing infrastructure through code and templates instead of manual configuration. You can start with Azure CLI or Azure PowerShell scripts and grow into repeatable environment deployments using Azure Resource Manager templates and Bicep. Because the environment is described in files rather than set up by hand, the same deployment can be repeated and gives consistent results each time.
author: claude

body: Azure Resource Manager (ARM) is the deployment and management service for Azure. It lets you create, update and delete resources, and every request from the portal, CLI, PowerShell or an SDK goes through it. An ARM template is a JSON file that declares the resources you want to deploy. Azure validates it and creates the resources in the right order. Templates give repeatable results across environments. Bicep is a simpler, more concise declarative language for deploying through ARM.
author: claude
